Figure 2.(a): An example BI dashboard built by users in the wild, extracted from a real Power BI project file (.pbix).
ForBI-Bench, we manually select a visualization whose title can accurately describe user intent: e.g., the visualization in the dashedpinkbox corresponds to a user questionQQ=‘‘Sales amount, budget, and forecast comparison by month and year’’.
(b): We directly retrieve the answerA⁡(Q)A(Q)forQQby exporting the underlying result table of the selected visualization as a CSV file through the “Export data” menu option (in thegreenbox). This(Q,A⁡(Q))(Q,A(Q))pair becomes the basis of a test case inBI-Bench.
(c): The input data tables of this BI project in a visual data model view. Note that this schema graph follows a “multi-snowflake” pattern common in BI, with the “Budget & Forecast” and “Sales” tables at the center serving as “fact tables” (inorangeboxes), and the remaining 7 tables serving as “dimension tables”.

Figure 3.(Left): a raw‘‘Sales’’table imported from spreadsheets. This is a “pivot table” in a cross-tabulation form and not properly relationalized, with different months as column headers, which makes it hard to perform relational analysis, such as joining on or aggregating over months. (Right): A properly relationalized version of the same‘‘Sales’’table, using theunpivottransformation, where both aggregating over and joining on‘‘Month’’become straightforward.
